identification.summary: Edalat-e Ali (Ali's Justice; also spelled Edalate Ali, Adalat Ali) is an anti-government hacktivist persona that has leaked security-camera footage and internal documents from Iranian prisons and the judiciary and has interrupted Iranian state broadcasts [S1][S3][S4][S5][S6]. RFE/RL reports the group describes itself as made up of Iranians living and working inside Iran, intent on exposing alleged human rights abuses and seeking the release of political prisoners; this is a self-description, not independently verified [S6].
identification.firstObserved: August 2021 (leak of Evin prison CCTV footage, the earliest incident in the sources gathered) [S1].
identification.notes: Name means 'Ali's Justice'. Not a Microsoft-named actor and no MITRE ATT&CK group. Do not merge with the separate January 2022 'EvilPlayout' intrusion into IRIB documented by Check Point, which that report does not attribute to this group [S7].

attribution.confidence: No government or vendor attribution of Edalat-e Ali to a state sponsor was found in the sources gathered. The group claims to be domestic Iranians opposed to the regime [S6]; this is unverified.
attribution.basis: Group's own claims and statements relayed by media (Iran International, RFE/RL) [S2][S3][S6]. Iranian officials confirmed the authenticity of the Evin footage [S1], and Tasnim acknowledged the October 2022 broadcast was 'hacked for a few moments by anti-revolutionary agents' [S4].

objectives: Expose alleged human rights abuses and judicial repression inside Iran, embarrass Iranian officials and state media, and encourage antigovernment protest [S1][S2][S4][S5][S6].

sectors: State broadcasting (IRIB streaming platform and news channel, state TV and radio)
targeting.notes: Evin prison CCTV footage released August 2021 [S1]; Ghezel Hesar prison videos and documents sent to Iran International in February 2022 [S3]; Telewebion live stream during an Iran-UAE football match on 2022-02-01 [S2]; state TV evening news on 2022-10-08 [S4]; Revolution Day speech by President Raisi on 2023-02-11 [S5]; judicial case-management documents released February 2024 [S6].

capabilities.summary: The sources show access to internal CCTV systems and prison computers (Evin, Ghezel Hesar), a judiciary case-management system holding more than 3 million documents (per the group's claim), and the ability to insert video and audio into live streams or broadcasts for seconds to about a minute [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5][S6]. Initial access methods, tooling and infrastructure are not described in the sources gathered. For October 2022, a state broadcaster spokesman said the incident was not a hack but internal 'vandalism and infiltration', so the technical means in that case are disputed [S4].

campaigns.name: Evin prison CCTV leak
campaigns.summary: Leaked videos from Tehran's Evin prison cameras showing guard abuse of prisoners were published by outside media starting 22 August 2021; Iran's prison chief acknowledged 'unacceptable behaviours' on 24 August and the judiciary later said cases were opened against guards. Hackers said the breach occurred months earlier.

campaigns.name: Telewebion live-stream hijack
campaigns.summary: Group interrupted the live stream of the state broadcaster's web platform during an Iran-UAE football match with a message urging protest.

campaigns.name: Ghezel Hesar prison leak
campaigns.summary: Group sent videos, files and prison documents to Iran International to demonstrate it had accessed Ghezel Hesar prison computers; documents reportedly listed prisoners arrested in the November 2019 protests.

campaigns.name: State TV news interruption
campaigns.summary: Evening news was briefly replaced with an image of Khamenei with crosshairs and flames and the text 'The blood of our youths is on your hands'; Tasnim acknowledged a brief hack while a broadcaster spokesman called it internal vandalism.

campaigns.name: Revolution Day speech disruption
campaigns.summary: Group disrupted the online broadcast of President Raisi's Revolution Day speech for about a minute, called for withdrawing money from government banks and joining protests on 16 February.

campaigns.name: Judiciary case-management leak
campaigns.summary: Group published a large set of documents from the judiciary's case management system, including Revolutionary Court Branch 26 material that RFE/RL says appears to show actions against Persian-language journalists abroad.

diamond.adversary: Self-described domestic anti-government hacktivists; membership, leadership and any outside support unknown [S6].
diamond.capability: Access to CCTV and internal prison and judiciary systems and to live broadcast or streaming feeds; exact techniques not reported [S1][S3][S5][S6].
diamond.victim: Iranian prisons, the judiciary, and state broadcasters (IRIB-related platforms and channels) [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Opposition to the Iranian government, timed to protest movements and national events such as Revolution Day and the 2022 protest wave [S4][S5][S6].
diamond.technology: Surveillance camera systems, prison and court IT systems, and live streaming or playout paths for state media [S1][S2][S5][S6].

gaps: Initial access, tools and infrastructure are not documented in the sources gathered; no technical report on this group was found.
Group identity, size and any state or foreign backing are unverified; only the group's self-description is available [S6].

Relationship to other Iranian opposition personas is unclear. One search summary stated that another hacktivist group, Tapandegan, promoted the Evin footage and credited Edalat-e Ali; the primary article was not opened.
An earlier debut action against Mashhad airport in May 2018 was mentioned in a search summary from a threat-intel profile; it was not confirmed in a source opened here.
Dates for the Evin hack itself are inconsistent across reports; only the leak date (August 2021) is supported [S1].
Whether the October 2022 incident was an external hack or insider action is disputed [S4].
Whether the group is linked to the January 2022 IRIB 'EvilPlayout' intrusion: Check Point's report treats that separately and no link is supported [S7].

Most pages could not be opened directly (fetch failures); several claims rest on search-result summaries of Iran International, RFE/RL, Al Jazeera and Check Point pages. Imported leads (Security Affairs, Hackread) were not read in full.
No Microsoft name or MITRE ATT&CK mapping exists for this group.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Iranian state broadcast chains, prison CCTV networks and judiciary case-management systems are the terrain the group has reached [S1][S3][S4][S6]. STEP 2: The actor is anti-regime and domestic by its own claim, so it is a regime-internal security problem, not a threat to US or coalition networks, based on the sources gathered [S6]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is access to an internal system, a later timed release or broadcast interruption tied to protests or national events, and delivery of material to diaspora media [S3][S5][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is further leaks and short broadcast disruptions timed to protest anniversaries and state events. MDCOA is a longer-duration takeover of broadcast or streaming systems during a crisis. Candidate indicators are unannounced protest-timing calls on social media, group logos on streams, and document dumps sent to Persian-language outlets [S2][S5][S6]. For US planners the main value is as an indicator of Iranian regime internal stability and information control, and as a source of open-source reporting; it is not a validated threat to DoD systems.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track the group's claims through open media and treat them as unverified until confirmed by officials or corroborating reporting, as with the Evin footage [S1][S6]. (2) Authorities: any US action touching this actor or Iranian networks would need separate legal review; the sources give no basis for operational action. (3) Mission assurance: no direct impact on US systems is shown in the sources. (4) Coordination: share notable disruptions with regional and IW or influence-analysis cells because activity is timed to political events [S4][S5].

provenance.importedSummary: Edalat-e Ali is a hacktivist group known for disrupting Iranian state-run TV and radio transmissions during significant events, such as the Revolution Day ceremonies. They have also targeted government facilities, releasing security camera footage to expose abuses and draw attention to human rights violations. The group has used their hacks to call for protests against the Iranian regime and have displayed anti-government messages during their disruptions. Edalat-e Ali has been active in releasing sensitive information and footage to embarrass Iranian officials and highlight injustices within the country.
